name: Red light LED mask

lead: A red light LED mask is a wearable panel that emits red and often near-infrared light, typically around 630 to 850 nanometers, against the face for several minutes at a time. It is a home version of low-level light therapy used in dermatology clinics.
It is marketed for fine lines, skin tone and texture, and post-procedure recovery, and is one of the better-studied home beauty device categories.

paras: Red and near-infrared light is absorbed by mitochondrial enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase in skin cells, which is thought to boost cellular energy and stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen while reducing inflammation. This process is called photobiomodulation.

Eye exposure is the main safety concern, so goggles or closed eyes are advised, and mild warmth or redness is possible. Sham-controlled trials show modest improvements in crow's feet and skin elasticity, but studies are small, often short and sometimes industry sponsored, and devices vary widely in dose and wavelength. Effects fade if treatment stops, and reported results are subtle.

lead: A red light LED mask is a wearable or handheld panel that delivers red light, and often near-infrared light, to the face for a few minutes per session. The technology is a consumer form of low-level light therapy, also called photobiomodulation (PBM), which applies low-power lasers or LEDs without damaging tissue.[1][2][3] Typical marketed wavelengths fall in the red (about 620-700 nm) and near-infrared (about 700-1440 nm) ranges.[4][2]

Masks are sold for fine lines, skin tone and texture, and recovery after procedures. A 2024 dermatology continuing-education review states that PBM is used effectively for conditions including acne, skin rejuvenation, wounds, scars and alopecia and describes it as having a favourable safety profile.[5] Home-device trials are fewer; a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study of a home LED and infrared mask for crow's feet was published in 2025, and a split-face pilot of a 637 and 854 nm home LED device appeared in 2020.[6][7]
Reviewers note that devices vary widely in wavelength and dose, and that trial sizes are modest and sometimes industry-linked.[5]
infobox: Low-level light therapy (LLLT), red light therapy
Small sham-controlled trials for crow's feet and rejuvenation

paras: Masks arrange LEDs across a face-shaped shell, while panels and wands are held at a distance. Many combine red (roughly 630-660 nm) and near-infrared (roughly 800-850 nm) diodes. Several photobiomodulation devices are cleared by the US FDA, according to Wikipedia's article on low-level laser therapy.[3]

Wikipedia credits Niels Finsen, who received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, as the father of modern light therapy; he used red light for smallpox lesions.[3] The Hungarian physician Endre Mester discovered biological effects of low-power lasers after the invention of the ruby laser in 1960 and the helium-neon laser in 1961; in a faulty-laser experiment on mice, shaved areas regrew hair faster, which he published in 1967.[3] He later reported accelerated wound healing and called the approach laser biostimulation, a term later superseded by low-level laser therapy and photobiomodulation.[3]

By 1987 companies selling lasers were claiming treatments for pain, sports injuries and arthritis with little supporting evidence, according to the same source, and in 2014 the FDA filed a complaint against one manufacturer, QLaser, for marketing devices for over 200 diseases; a permanent injunction followed in 2015.[3] LED masks for cosmetic use are a later consumer development of the same technology.

Photobiomodulation theory holds that light must be absorbed to act, and the generally accepted candidate is cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial respiratory chain.[3] A 2024 review describes red and near-infrared absorption by this enzyme as modulating mitochondrial ATP, reactive oxygen species and intracellular calcium, which in turn activate signalling pathways such as those involving insulin-like growth factor.[4] In skin, this is proposed to stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen and to reduce inflammation.[4] Wikipedia notes that doses below an effective range do not appear to work, and that effects seem limited to certain wavelengths.[3]

A 2024 dermatology review states that PBM can be effective in acne, rejuvenation, wounds and scars among other conditions.[5] Evidence for home masks is narrower. A 2025 multicentre, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial examined a home LED and infrared mask for crow's feet.[6] The 2020 split-face pilot tested a home LED device at 637 and 854 nm for facial rejuvenation.[7] A 2023 article in Skin Research and Technology discussed red-light PBM and signs of skin aging.[8] Authors of this literature commonly note small samples, short follow-up and variable dosing, and trial results suggest subtle rather than dramatic changes.[5][6]

Wikipedia reports mild pain or skin irritation after red-light therapy and states that long-term effects on skin or hair are not known; eye protection is suggested for some devices.[3] A 2023 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal assessed the oncologic safety of low-level light therapy for aesthetic rejuvenation, and Wikipedia summarises a systematic review finding no evidence that people with cancer or at risk of cancer should avoid PBM.[9][3] Clinical guidelines cited there suggest consulting a dermatologist first and using devices authorised by the relevant regulator.[3]

Repeated low-level red-light therapy has been studied extensively for slowing myopia in children. A multicentre randomized trial of 264 children aged 8 to 13, a trial in high-myopia children, a double-blind sham-controlled trial of 112 children, and a network meta-analysis of atropine, orthokeratology and red light are among the reports.[10][11][12][13] These use specialised low-power laser devices under clinical supervision and do not evaluate cosmetic masks.

Human studies of home masks include a 2025 multicentre, double-blind, sham-controlled trial for crow's feet[6] and a 2020 split-face pilot study at 637 and 854 nm.[7] Professional-device and review literature for acne, wound healing and rejuvenation is summarised in dermatology reviews.[5][4] Research on myopia and other conditions is a separate use and is not evidence about facial appearance.[10][11]
